directions.question: How do teams with distributed decision authority revise shared task knowledge following disruption?
directions.logical_move: P(S,C)? → P′(S,C)?, where P′ is revising shared task knowledge.

fixed.S: Organizational teams with decision authority distributed among members or constituent units to some degree.
fixed.C: After a disruption; event severity, duration and boundaries remain unspecified.
fixed.scope: Non-coercive organizational coordination; exclude employee surveillance and military command.

changed.P: Regaining alignment capacity → revising shared task knowledge.

directions.discovery_target: Learning activities and evidence of changed shared understanding after an event; do not count restored coordination as proof of learning.

directions.bridge_test: Verify that an observed team actually distributes relevant decision authority, that disruption precedes knowledge revision, and that knowledge changes are measured independently of coordination outcomes. A hierarchical surgical-team example alone fails the subject bridge.
directions.novelty_reason: A team may acquire or revise knowledge while coordination remains impaired, or restore alignment without revising its task knowledge. This is a neighboring cognitive process rather than another label for recovery.
directions.finding: A qualitative study of 16 hospitals implementing a cardiac-surgery technology describes different team learning processes among successful and unsuccessful implementers. The paper supports studying learning under disrupted routines, but does not establish the anchor’s distributed-authority subject.
unknowns: Whether the relevant hospital teams meet S.
Whether voluntary knowledge revision after disruption also occurs when authority is distributed.
Learning indicators, timing, and causal direction.

directions.question: How do teams with distributed decision authority distribute scarce resources among competing member or unit claims following disruption?
directions.logical_move: P(S,C)? → P′(S,C)?, where P′ is allocating scarce resources among claims.

fixed.S: Organizational teams with decision authority distributed among members or constituent units to some degree.
fixed.C: After a disruption; no new assumption that all disruptions create scarcity.
fixed.scope: Non-coercive organizational coordination; exclude employee surveillance and military command.

changed.P: Regaining alignment capacity → resource allocation outcomes and allocation authority in episodes where competing claims exist.

directions.discovery_target: Allocation rules, resulting distribution and reasons accepted for competing claims; scarcity is a case characteristic to verify rather than a new universal condition.

directions.bridge_test: Within a team or constituent-unit collective satisfying S, identify a disruption and trace actual competing resource claims, decision rights and allocations. Separate the amount or distributive pattern allocated from whether interdependent work becomes aligned. Do not infer that an organization-wide ethnography automatically establishes a team-level post-event relation.
directions.novelty_reason: An allocation can be more unequal or more efficient while the team remains equally coordinated. The target is the distribution of resources and authority over that distribution, not recovered alignment.
directions.finding: An 18-month ethnography examines enactments and reversions of decentralized authority in an organization granting role holders decision authority without managerial approval. It offers a subject/authority framing, but the retrieved text does not establish a post-disruption scarce-resource allocation relationship at team level.

candidate_validity.semantic: valid if allocation is assessed as a distinct distribution outcome

unknowns: Which allocation decisions remain within distributed authority.
Whether and when a disruption produces competing claims.
Team boundary and non-coercive allocation rules.
No direct target evidence verified within retrieval budget.

fixed.C: After disruption; do not presume disruption entails conflict or a trust violation.
fixed.scope: Non-coercive organizational coordination; exclude employee surveillance and military command.

changed.P: Regaining alignment capacity → changes in willingness to rely on teammates and expectations of their conduct.

directions.bridge_test: Check actual distribution of decision authority and a temporally defined disruption; measure trust independently. Conflict in the source is not automatically C, and a conflict–trust association does not prove a general post-disruption process.
directions.novelty_reason: Trust concerns relational expectations and vulnerability; teams can align through explicit agreements despite low trust. Neither trust recovery nor trust decline is synonymous with recovering coordination.
directions.finding: The publisher abstract for a longitudinal self-managing-team study proposes that conflict relates to lower intrateam trust, with possible reductions in autonomy and task interdependence. This provides a distinct relational question, not verified evidence for a disruption-to-trust mechanism in the anchor population.

candidate_validity.scope_fit: self-managing subject is relevant; authority details and disruption bridge unverified

unknowns: Full methods and results inaccessible through attempted open.
Whether the source’s conflict episodes meet C.
Whether changed autonomy means the same teams cease to satisfy S over time.

directions.bridge_test: Confirm decision authority is distributed in the studied production teams or locate another organizational sample meeting S. Measure expression and uptake before testing any link to coordination. Performance trajectories cannot substitute for coordination evidence.
directions.novelty_reason: Speaking up is an observable communication behavior that may be ignored or occur without restored alignment; the target can be investigated even if no recovery occurs.
directions.finding: The author abstract reports a field study of 172 production teams and an experiment with 88 teams supporting different roles for warning-oriented and improvement-oriented voice around exogenous change. directions.bridge_test: Verify that autonomy includes distributed decision authority, identify an actual interruption episode rather than continuous environmental turbulence alone, and score novelty/usefulness separately from coordination and shared-knowledge change.
directions.novelty_reason: Innovation concerns outputs; learning concerns changed knowledge. A team can regain coordination and learn without producing a novel useful output, or innovate while alignment remains fragile.
directions.finding: Publisher-indexed text of two field studies reports relationships among technological turbulence, acquisition of new knowledge, reduced dependence on established experts, and innovation performance; team autonomy strengthens the reported mediated relationships. The post-disruption temporal sequence and distributed authority bridge remain unverified.

candidate_validity.semantic: valid predicate change, distinct from learning and recovery
candidate_validity.scope_fit: autonomy and turbulence require explicit bridges to S and C

unknowns: Whether team autonomy means decision authority distributed within the team.
Whether turbulence constitutes a discrete disruption in observed cases.
Causal interpretation of the reported mediation.
